newsitem.title: USA: Primergy parties reviewing U.S. FERC order.
newsitem.headline: Primergy parties reviewing U.S. FERC order.

text.p: Wisconsin Energy Corp and Northern States Power Co officials Wednesday said they needed to review federal regulators' requirements that they find more ways to reduce market power in their merger plan.

"We're going to take some time in the next few days to review this, but we're looking at this that FERC (the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission) didn't either approve or deny our application. It established a settlement procedure for us to resolve the issues related to generation market power," a Wisconsin Energy spokeswoman said.

Northern States withheld comment after the FERC gave the two companies three months to come up with a plan to ease the commission's concerns that their merger into a utility called Primergy would concentrate market power too much.
The commission told the two upper Midwestern utilities to negotiate ways to mitigate market power in a three-month settlement hearing. FERC then would evaluate the settlement judge's finding.
"We give the parties one more bite at the apple" in a settlement conference "for purposes of exploring ways to remedy the generation market power problem," Commissioner Donald Santa said.

The commission in a statement said generation plant divestiture in the Wisconsin-Upper Michigan Systems "may offer a particularly useful approach to mitigate its market power concerns in the highly concentrated market."
The commission accepted the utilities' proposal to form an independent systems operator, but wanted changes in the plan to strengthen the ISO and increase its independence.
It also said it expected the companies to participate in any state-wide or regional ISO.
The commission's ruling reversed last summer's findings by an administrative law judge who said the merger would not significantly increase the utilities' market power.
The utilities' filed the merger application 22 months ago, before the commission adopted merger policies.
The merger would create the nation's tenth largest utility which would serve more than 3 million people in Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, North Dakota and South Dakota.
